newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Three letter bombs sent to Arab newspaper at U.N..
newsitem.headline: Three letter bombs sent to Arab newspaper at U.N..

text.p: United Nations security staff sifted letters and parcels throughout the night after finding three letter bombs addressed to the U.N. bureau of an an Arab-language newspaper. No one was injured.
The third letter bomb, discovered late on Monday, like the two previous ones, was addressed to the U.N. bureau of the Arabic-language newspaper Al-Hayat.
"They have dismantled the third one. It was live like the other two," U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard told Reuters.
U.N. security chief Michael McCann summoned the New York police bomb squad for a third time on Monday to dismantle the device in U.N. headquarters on New York's East River.
"It was identical to the other two" and also addressed to Al-Hayat, Eckhard added. "Security and regular mailroom personnel are combing the mail all night long,"
An estimated 20,000 pieces of mail reach the United Nations daily.

Earlier on Monday a bomb exploded at the London headquarters of Al-Hayat, owned by a Saudi Arabian, wounding two security guards. Four more suspected devices were subsequently found there, British police said.

The letters at the United Nations were similar to those mailed earlier this month to the newspaper's Washington bureau. U.N. sources said the letters, like those received in Washington, bore an Alexandria, Egypt, postmark.

U.N. officials would not say where the third letter had been discovered. The suspicious envelope was among those taken to the General Assembly area where an electronic scanner, usually used to screen tourists, was used to supplement the one in the main basement mail room.

The letter bombs were contained in greeting card-sized envelopes. The first was found about 11 a.m. (1600 GMT) in a second-floor messenger room, about 15 minutes before it would have been delivered, Eckhard said. The second one was discovered in the basement mail room several hours later.

It was addressed to the Al-Hayat's bureau, not to any specific individual. U.N. security was on the lookout for mail addressed to Al-Hayat after its U.N. correspondent, Raghida Dergham, informed them of the London incident.
After the first suspicious envelope was found, parts of two floors of the 38-floor complex were closed and part of the press area was evacuated.

Secretary-General Kofi Annan told reporters as he left the building, "We consider it an attack on the organisation and also on freedom of press and speech. We hope that whoever has undertaken this cowardly act will cease before some serious damage is done."

"This is a house of peace and we work in the interest of all nations," he said, adding: This kind of activity is not something that anyone can condone and I appeal to them to desist and use other means to raise their complaints."
The FBI launched an investigation earlier this month after eight letter bombs made to look like Christmas cards were mailed from Egypt to the United States.
Four arrived at Al-Hayat's Washington office and a fifth was found in the mail system. Three other devices turned up in the area around Leavenworth federal prison in Kansas.

Mohammad Salameh, a militant Moslem jailed for life for the 1993 World Trade Centre bombing, is in Leavenworth, as are Victor Alvarez and Mohammed Saleh who were convicted of plotting to blow up U.N. headquarters and other targets.
